{{1964 Winter Olympics}}
The '''1964 Winter Olympics''', officially known as the '''IX Olympic Winter Games''' ({{langx|de|IX. Olympische Winterspiele}}) and commonly known as '''Innsbruck 1964''' ({{langx|bar|Innschbruck 1964|label=[[Bavarian language|Austro-Bavarian]]}}), were a winter [[multi-sport event]] which was celebrated in [[Innsbruck]], Austria, from January 29 to February 9, 1964. The city was already an Olympic candidate, unsuccessfully bidding to host the [[1960 Winter Olympic Games|1960 Games]]. Innsbruck won the 1964 Games bid, defeating the cities of [[Calgary]] in Canada and [[Lahti]] in Finland. The sports venues, many of which were built for the Games, were located within a radius of {{convert|20|km|abbr=on}} around Innsbruck. The Games included 1,091 athletes from 36 nations, which was a record for the Winter Games at the time. Athletes participated in six [[Olympic sports|sports]] and ten disciplines which bring together a total of thirty-four official events, seven more than the [[1960 Winter Olympic Games]]. The [[Luge at the 1964 Winter Olympics|luge]] made its debut on the Olympic program. Three Asian nations made their Winter Games debut: [[North Korea at the 1964 Winter Olympics|North Korea]], [[India at the 1964 Winter Olympics|India]] and [[Mongolia at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Mongolia]].

The [[Soviet Union at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Soviet Union]] broke the record for the most gold and overall medals at a single Winter Olympics, with eleven and twenty five respectively, and finished first in the [[1964 Winter Olympics medal table|medal table]]. The USSR was followed by [[Austria at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Austria]], the host country, which won twelve medals, four of which were gold. Soviet athletes [[Lidia Skoblikova]] won all four women's races of [[Speed skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics|speed skating]] and [[Klavdiya Boyarskikh]] won all three events of [[Cross-country skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics|cross-country skiing]]. The Swedish cross-country skier [[Sixten Jernberg]], a three-time medalist at these Games, became the first athlete to collect nine medals at the Winter Games. In [[Alpine skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics|alpine skiing]], the French sisters [[Christine Goitschel|Christine]] and [[Marielle Goitschel]] each obtained a gold and a silver medal. Before the Games, the Austrian army was mobilized to deal with the lack of snow. They brought thousands of cubic meters of it from [[Brenner Pass]], close to the Italian border. The Olympic Winter Games was held for a second time at Innsbruck in [[1976 Winter Olympic Games|1976]].

The [[Olympic Flame|Olympic Torch]] was carried by [[Josl Rieder|Joseph Rieder]],<ref>"Olympic Winter Games Innsbruck 1964" (history), kiat.net, webpage:
     [http://kiat.net/olympics/history/winter/w09innsbruck.html KIAT-Innsbruck] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061109184007/http://www.kiat.net/olympics/history/winter/w09innsbruck.html |date=2006-11-09 }}.</ref> a former [[alpine skier]] who had participated in the [[1956 Winter Olympics]].

The Games were affected by the deaths of Australian alpine skier [[Ross Milne (alpine skier)|Ross Milne]] and [[Great Britain|British]] [[luge]] slider [[Kazimierz Kay-Skrzypeski]], during training, and by the deaths, [[Sabena Flight 548|three years earlier]], of the entire United States [[figure skating]] team and family members.

== Bid and background for the Games ==
=== Host city selection ===
The city of [[Innsbruck]] submitted its first Olympic bid in the 1950s to host the [[1960 Winter Olympic Games]]. The Austrians had a convincing bid and were viewed as the favorites to host the games. However, in the second round of the vote the members of the [[International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) selected the American city of [[Squaw Valley, Placer County, California|Squaw Valley]] due to its ambitious designs.<ref name=universalis>{{cite web |url=https://www.universalis.fr/encyclopedie/innsbruck-jeux-olympiques-d-1964-contexte-organisation-bilan/ |title=Innsbruck (Olympic Games) 1964 – Context, organization, report |author=Pierre Lagrue |editor=[[Encyclopædia Universalis]] |access-date=January 12, 2014 |url-access=registration |language=french}}</ref><ref>{{harvsp|Adams|2004|p=345}}</ref>

A month later, the Innsbruck authorities decided to enter a bid again for the 1964 Winter Games.<ref>{{harvsp | Wolfgang | Neumann | 1967 | p = 9}}</ref> On 26 May 1959, during the 55th session of the (IOC) in [[Munich]], [[West Germany]], the Austrians were selected in a landslide for the Games with 49 votes in the first round, ahead of [[Calgary]] ([[Canada]]), which obtained 9 votes and [[Lahti]] ([[Finland]]), which did not receive a vote.<ref name=universalis /><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aldaver.com/votes.html |title=the International Olympic Committee Vote History |access-date=2008-06-10 |archive-date=2008-05-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080525070757/http://www.aldaver.com/votes.html |url-status=usurped}}</ref>

=== Political situation ===
Despite the construction of the [[Berlin Wall]] by East Germany in 1961, which increased tensions between East and West and the fact that the East Germans wanted to have their own team, the {{abbreviation | IOC | International Olympic Committee}} managed to maintain the [[United Team of Germany at the Olympics|United Team of Germany]] for the third consecutive Olympiad.<ref>{{harvsp | Espy | 1981 | p = 77}}</ref> In the 1960s, the IOC also discussed the Olympic participation of [[South Africa at the Olympics|South Africa]], a country immersed in the [[apartheid]] regime. During the Games in Innbruck, the IOC President [[Avery Brundage]] announced that the country would not be able to participate in the [[1964 Summer Olympics]] because of its policy of racial segregation in sport.<ref>{{harvsp|Espy|1981|p=87}}</ref> On the other hand, several African countries which had become independent joined the Olympic movement: the [[National Olympic Committee|national Olympic committees]] of [[Algeria at the Olympics|Algeria]], of [[Republic of the Congo at the Olympics|Congo]], from [[Nigeria at the Olympics|Nigeria]] and [[Sierra Leone at the Olympics|Sierra Leone]] were recognized by the IOC during the session held during the Innsbruck Games. The number of IOC member nations increased to 114.<ref name="Adams p.348" /> In addition, the Innsbruck Games were used for the dissemination of political messages. Five Iranian students were arrested after marching with banners hostile to the [[shah]]. Twenty other Iranians, who demonstrated for the release of prisoners in their country, were also imprisoned.<ref name="Adams p.349" />

== Organization ==
=== Organizing Committee ===
The Organizing Committee of the IX Winter Olympics in Innsbruck 1964 was formed on 2 June 1959. [[Heinrich Drimmel]], President of the [[Austrian Olympic Committee]] and [[Federal Ministry of Education, Science and Research|Federal Minister of Education]], was elected as its president and Friedl Wolfgang was elected as its secretary-general. The organizing committee was made up of the general assembly, the board of directors, and the executive committee, as well as eight sub-committees created to manage the different aspects of the Games: finance, construction, sports, transport, etc. accommodation and medical services, lodging, administration and checks.<ref>{{harvsp | Wolfgang | Neumann | 1967 | pp = 11–12}}</ref>

=== Financial aspects ===
The Innsbruck Games cost around one billion [[Austrian schilling|schillings]], or 40 million [[US dollar]]s distributed among the organizing committee, the Austrian state, the Land of Tyrol and the city of Innsbruck.<ref name="Adams p.346" /><ref>{{cite journal |language=de |trans-title=Austria / Olympic Games: New switches |title=Österreich / Olympische Spiele: Neue Schalter |journal=[[Der Spiegel]] |date=January 14, 1964 |url=http://www.spiegel.de/spiegel/print/d-46162725.html |access-date=January 16, 2014}}</ref> The organizers tried to reduce the expenses related to the provisional elements, and to invest more money for the facilities which would continue to be used after the Games.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Les IXes Jeux Olympiques d'Hiver Innsbruck 1964 |journal=Olympic Review |year=1962 |url=http://library.la84.org/OlympicInformationCenter/RevueOlympique/1962/BDCF77/BDCF77i.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160826063449/http://library.la84.org/OlympicInformationCenter/RevueOlympique/1962/BDCF77/BDCF77i.pdf |archive-date=26 August 2016 |access-date=January 16, 2014}}</ref> The [[Olympiahalle (Innsbruck)|Olympiaeisstadion]] costs 75 million schillings, the renovation of the [[Bergisel Ski Jump]] 15 million and the [[Olympic Sliding Centre Innsbruck]] 10 million. The development of ski slopes, cross-country skiing and biathlon required a total of 29&nbsp;million. The Olympic village, intended to become a leisure center, costs 174&nbsp;million. A total of 225&nbsp;million was invested to renovate and develop the road network in the region.<ref>{{harvsp | Wolfgang | Neumann | 1967 | pp = 252–253}}</ref>

=== Television ===
The 1964 edition was the third time that the Winter Games were broadcast on television and the second time that exclusive broadcasting rights were sold. This was a substantial increase: where they were {{currency | 50000 | US}} in [[1960 Winter Olympic Games|1960]], the broadcast rights yielded {{currency | 937000 | US}} in 1964, which was approximately 24 million [[Austrian schilling|schillings]]. Thirty countries broadcast the Games. The American channel [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] paid nearly 15.4&nbsp;million schillings, or 64 per cent of the broadcast rights revenue. The [[Eurovision (network)|Eurovision]] network spent around 7.6&nbsp;million for 16 countries, the Soviet television 600,000&nbsp;[[Soviet rouble|Rbls]] and the Intervision network {{currency | 550000}} for six countries in Western Europe.<ref>{{harvsp | Monnin | 2010 | p = 203}}</ref><ref>{{harvsp | Wolfgang | Neumann | 1967 | p = 256}}</ref> The [[CTV Television Network]] paid {{currency | 5000 | CAD}} for the exclusive broadcast rights in Canada.<ref>{{cite news |title=OCO'88 plans TV rights campaign |work=[[Calgary Herald]] |date=August 23, 1985 |page=B2 |id={{ProQuest|2259003643}}}}</ref>

== Schedule ==
=== Calendar ===
The Games were held over twelve days, from January 29 to February 9. Thirty-four events were on the program, an increase from the twenty-seven at Squaw Valley four years earlier. Three [[Luge at the 1964 Winter Olympics|luge]] events (individual men and women, doubles men) were included in the Olympic program. [[Bobsleigh at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Bobsled]], which was absent from the 1960 Games due to the cost of building the track, returned to the Games. [[Ski jumping at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Ski jumping]] was divided into two events (small and large hill) and the women's 5-kilometer was added in [[Cross-country skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics|cross-country skiing]].<ref name=universalis /> [[Ice stock sport]] (Eisstockschießen), a variant of curling popular in Alpine countries, was a [[demonstration sport]] as in [[Garmisch-Partenkirchen]] in [[Eisstock at the 1936 Olympic Games|1936]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |url=https://www.britannica.com/sports/Eisstockschiessen |title=Eisstockschiessen |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]] |access-date=June 8, 2021}}</ref> In total, 1,073,000 people attend the various events. The disciplines which attracted the most spectators were alpine skiing and ice hockey.<ref name=cio>{{cite web |title=Monti's Olympic spirit rewarded with double gold |url=https://olympics.com/en/news/monti-s-olympic-spirit-rewarded-with-double-gold |publisher=International Olympic Committee |access-date=8 June 2021 |date=14 February 1968}}</ref>

=== Weather conditions before the Games ===
In the weeks leading up to the Games, temperatures often rose above zero degrees Celsius due to the [[foehn]], a hot, dry wind. There was no major snowfall for seven weeks, and the rain melted snow and ice at sports venues. This was the first time in around a century that the snowfall had been so low in Tyrol.<ref name=universalis /><ref name="Adams p.346" /> Two weeks before the start of the Games, thousands of Austrian soldiers were mobilized to transport by truck 40,000m3 of snow from the [[Brenner Pass]], close to the Italian border, and spread it by hand on the ski slopes. 20,000m3 of snow was built up and 20,000 blocks of ice were transported to the bobsleigh and toboggan run.<ref name="Adams p.346" /><ref>{{harvsp | Mogore | 1989 | p = 95}}</ref><ref>{{harvsp | Wallechinsky | 2001 | p = xiv}}</ref>

=== Opening Ceremony ===
[[File:Josl Rieder 1964 Olympic cauldron.jpg|thumb|right|Winter Olympics open in Innsbruck, [[Josl Rieder]] lights the Olympic Caldron ]]

The Opening Ceremony took place on January 29 at the [[Bergisel Ski Jump]] stadium in front of approximately 50,000 spectators. The Games were opened by the [[President of Austria]] [[Adolf Schärf]]. The bobsledder [[Paul Aste]] took the [[Olympic oath]]. Aste modified the oath slightly: instead of saying "for the glory of sport and the honor of our countries", he replaced the word "country" with "teams" to remove the nationalist elements of the oath. This was the first time that the [[Olympic flame]] of the Winter Games has been lit in front of the Temple of Hera in [[Olympia, Greece|Olympia]], Greece. In the stadium, the alpine skier [[Josl Rieder|Josef Rieder]] lit the cauldron. Tyrolean orchestras performed during the ceremony.<ref name="universalis chronology">{{cite web |url=http://www.universalis.fr/encyclopedie/1964-9es-jeux-olympiques-d-hiver/ |language=French |title=Innsbruck (Olympic Games) 1964 – Chronology |author=Pierre Lagrue |editor=[[Encyclopædia Universalis]] |access-date=June 8, 2021}}</ref><ref name="1964 Innsbruck Winter Games" /><ref name="Adams p.347">{{harvsp | Adams | 2004 | p = 347}}</ref>

== Events ==
=== Biathlon ===
{{Main|Biathlon at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}

The [[biathlon]] made its second Olympic appearance. As in 1960, the only event contested was a 20-kilometer cross-country ski race with four shooting ranges of 100 to 250 meters. Soviet athlete [[Vladimir Melanin]], a heavy favorite, won the event. This was the first time he did not miss any of his twenty shots in a major competition. His compatriot [[Aleksandr Privalov]], who also had a clean shoot, was second by more than three minutes and the Norwegian [[Olav Jordet]], who missed a target, won the bronze medal. The Finn [[Veikko Hakulinen]] was the fastest, but missed six shots and finished 15th.<ref>{{cite web |title=Biathlon at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/BIA |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021 |archive-date=8 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210608154205/https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/BIA |url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Bobsleigh ===
[[File:Bobsleigh World Cup Igls 2011.jpg|thumb|alt=View of the bobsleigh track | The [[Olympic Sliding Centre Innsbruck]] in 2011.]]
{{Main|Bobsleigh at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}
The [[bobsleigh]] was not on the program for the [[1960 Winter Olympic Games]], at Squaw Valley in the United States, because of the low number of crews and the cost of building the track. In 1964, bobsleigh events made a comeback and were contested on the [[Olympic Sliding Centre Innsbruck]]. Neither of the two Olympic champion teams, Great Britain and Canada, had a track in their country at the time.<ref name="Bobsleigh at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games">{{cite web |title=Bobsleigh at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/BOB |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

During the first round of the two-man event, the bobsleigh of the British [[Robin Dixon]] and [[Tony Nash (bobsledder)|Tony Nash]] was damaged and the competition's favorite, the Italian [[Eugenio Monti]], lent them an axle bolt. After two rounds, the British beat the two Italian teams. After the third set, the Italians [[Sergio Zardini]] and [[Romano Bonagura]] beat Dixon and Nash by just five hundredths of a second. Finally, Dixon and Nash become Olympic champions with 12 hundredths ahead of silver medalists Zardini and Bonagura and 73 over third, Eugenio Monti and [[Sergio Siorpaes]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Two, Men – 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/309 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> This is the only time in history that the British have been Olympic bobsleigh champions. After the Games, Monti received the first [[International Fair Play Committee]] Pierre de Coubertin World Trophy for his sportsmanship towards the British team.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/how-many-athletes-have-won-the-pierre-de-coubertin-medal-2016-8 |title=There are 2 prestigious awards named for the founder of the modern Olympic movement – here are 8 athletes who have won them |last=Praderio |first=Caroline |date=23 August 2016 |website=Business Insider |access-date=9 August 2024}}</ref>

The Canadians surprised in the four-man bobsleigh event. As the country competed for the first time in the Olympic bobsleigh events,<ref>{{harvsp | Wallechinsky | 2001 | p = 167}}</ref> the pilot's team [[Vic Emery]] won the first round, breaking the track record, and increased his lead in the following three rounds. Canada won gold by more than a second ahead of [[Erwin Thaler]] 's Austrian bobsleigh and Eugenio Monti' s Italian bobsleigh.<ref>{{cite web |title=Four, Men – 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/316 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

=== Nordic combined ===
{{Main|Nordic combined at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}
The [[Nordic combined]] event took place in the village of [[Seefeld in Tirol]]. On the first day, the competitors did three jumps and the two best results are recorded. The next day, they did a 15-kilometer cross-country ski race. The final ranking was established with a new points system.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nordic Combined at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/NCO |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021 |archive-date=8 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210608160330/https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/NCO |url-status=dead}}</ref>

The reigning Olympic champion, the German [[Georg Thoma]], was first ahead of the Norwegian [[Tormod Knutsen]] and the Soviet [[Nikolay Kiselyov (athlete)|Nikolay Kiselyov]] after the jumps. Knutsen needed to beat Thoma by at least twelve seconds in the cross-country ski race to pass him, which he did, winning by 1.33 and becoming Olympic champion. Kisseliov wins the silver medal. Thoma, who had wax problems and fell twice during the race, was third, just 0.16 points behind Kisseliov after a tenth-place finish in cross-country skiing.<ref>{{cite web |title=Individual, Men – 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/2231 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

=== Ice hockey ===
{{Main|Ice hockey at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}

The matches of [[ice hockey]] were played in the [[Olympiahalle (Innsbruck)|Olympiaeisstadion]] and the [[Messehalle (Innsbruck)|Messehalle]]. The sixteen participating teams first played a match to determine their group for the rest of the competition: group A (which allocates places 1 to 8) or group B (places 9 to 16). Then, each team faced the other seven of its group.<ref name="Ice Hockey at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games">{{cite web |title=Ice Hockey at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/ICH |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021 |archive-date=8 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210608160319/https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/ICH |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In Group A, the Soviet favorites won their seven matches and became Olympic champions. The tournament was actually very close since in the last game, the Soviets were losing 2–1 against Canada after two periods to finally win 3–2; if Canada had won they would have taken the gold medal. Behind the Soviet Union, three teams had five wins and two losses: Canada, Czechoslovakia and Sweden. These three teams were ranked by goal difference with Sweden receiving silver, Czechoslovakia bronze and Canada finishing fourth.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ice Hockey, Men – 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/20280 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> The Canadians, who were not satisfied with the method used to decide between Sweden and Czechoslovakia, boycotted the medal ceremony.<ref name="Adams p.349">{{harvsp | Adams | 2004 | p = 349}}</ref>

=== Luge ===
[[File:Bundesarchiv Bild 183-C0223-0007-002, Ortrun Enderlein.jpg|thumb|right|Olympic champion [[Ortrun Enderlein]] shortly after the Games.]]

{{Main|Luge at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}

[[Luge]] was a popular sport in the Alpine countries, the first competition of which dates back to 1831. The first international event was organized in 1928. The {{abbreviation | IOC | International Olympic Committee}} decided in 1954 to include luge in the program of the 1964 Games to replace the [[skeleton (sport)|skeleton]], because there was only one track adapted to this sport: the [[Cresta Run]] of [[Saint-Moritz]] in Switzerland.<ref group="N">The skeleton would only be part of the Olympic program again in [[Skeleton at the 2002 Olympic Games|2002]]</ref> Three events were contested at the Games: individual for men and women and two for men. Some commentators believed that luge was too dangerous a sport to enter the Olympic program. The death of Poland-born British luger [[Kazimierz Kay-Skrzypeski]] during a test run two weeks before the start of the Games helped reinforce this position.

The luge events were dominated by the Germans, who took five out of six medals individually.<ref>{{cite web |title=Luge at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/LUG |website=Olmpedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref><ref>{{harvsp | Wallechinsky | 2001 | p = 172}}</ref> During the men's individual event, a German trio dominated the competition: the 1962 world champion [[Thomas Köhler]] as well as [[Klaus Bonsack]] and [[Hans Plenk]] were the top three in each of the first three rounds, won respectively by Köhler, Bonsack and again Köhler. Bonsack also won the fourth round. Finally, Köhler became an Olympic champion, 27 hundredths of a second ahead of Bonsack and 3.38 seconds ahead of Plenk.<ref>{{cite web |title=Singles, Men – 1964 Winter Olympic Games |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/29 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

The German [[Ilse Geisler]], world champion in 1962 and 1963, was the favorite in the women's event. However, it was her compatriot [[Ortrun Enderlein]] who won the first three races. Geiser took a lot of risks in the last heat and made a big mistake, letting Enderlein win again. Enderlein became Olympic champion, almost three seconds ahead of Geisler. The Austrian [[Helene Thurner]] won the bronze medal.<ref>{{cite web |title=Singles, Women – 1964 Winter Olympic Games |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/39 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

The doubles event, which takes place over two rounds, was dominated by the Austrians. Indeed, [[Josef Feistmantl]] and [[Manfred Stengl]] won the first round ahead of [[Reinhold Senn]] and [[Helmut Thaler]]. The latter won the second round without worrying Feistmantl and Stengl, crowned Olympic champions. Italians [[Walter Ausserdorfer]] and [[Sigisfredo Mair]] are bronze medalists.<ref>{{cite web |title=Doubles, Open – 1964 Winter Olympic Games |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/36 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

=== Figure skating ===
{{Main|Figure skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}

[[File:Olympische Spelen 1964 te Innsbruck, Sjoukje Dijkstra tijdens kur, Bestanddeelnr 916-0188.jpg|thumb|left|Dutch Figure Skater [[Sjoukje Dijkstra]] practicing at the 1964 Olympics]]

The [[figure skating]] events were held at the [[Olympiahalle (Innsbruck)|Olympiaeisstadion]]. Individually, men and women performed a free skate and compulsory figures while, for the last time in an international competition, the couples only presented one program.<ref>{{cite web |title=Figure Skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/FSK |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> Computers are used for refereeing, which is new to the Olympics. The data processing system provided by the company [[International Business Machines|IBM]] allows scores to be announced instantly. In addition to figure skating, information is sent to a [[data center]] at [[University of Innsbruck]] from eleven other facilities.<ref>{{harvsp | Adams | 2004 | pp= 347–348}}</ref>

In the men's event, the German [[Manfred Schnelldorfer]] became Olympic champion by winning each round. The Frenchman [[Alain Calmat]], slightly favored before the Olympics, finished in second place.<ref>{{cite web |title=Singles, Men – Figure Skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/13112 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> The American [[Scott Allen (figure skater)|Scott Allen]] won the bronze medal, just two days before his fifteenth birthday. He thus became the youngest medalist in the history of the Winter Games.<ref>{{harvsp | Wallechinsky | 2001 |p=42}}</ref>

The big favorite in the women's event, the Dutch [[Sjoukje Dijkstra]], easily became Olympic champion. She is in fact placed in the first row by the nine judges. In front of the Dutch royal family, she won the first Dutch gold medal at the Winter Games. The Austrian [[Regine Heitzer]] was the silver medalist with a small lead over the Canadian [[Petra Burka]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Singles, Women – Figure Skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/13142 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="Valle p.100">{{harvsp | Valle | 1988 | p = 100}}</ref>

The Soviets [[Ludmila Belousova]] and [[Oleg Protopopov]], a married couple, narrowly won the pair event ahead of the German [[Marika Kilius]] and [[Hans-Jürgen Bäumler]]. The bronze medals went to Canadians [[Debbi Wilkes]] and [[Guy Revell]]. In 1966, Kilius and Bäumler had to return their medals because of a professional contract signed before the Games. The Canadians received the silver medal and the Americans [[Vivian Joseph|Vivian]] and [[Ronald Joseph (figure skater)|Ronald Joseph]], initially fourth, received the bronze medal. In 1987, however, the {{abbreviation | IOC | International Olympic Committee}} decided to restore the medals of the German couple. The results then plunged into confusion since the different rankings did not indicate the same information. In 2013, the IOC clarified that the Soviets had the gold medal, the Canadians and the Germans shared the silver medal and the Americans the bronze medal. These were the official results since 1987.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pairs, Mixed – Figure Skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/13172 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first1=Amy |last1=Rosewater |title=1964 Olympic Skating Pair Only Now Discovering Their Place |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=13 December 2013 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/12/14/sports/olympics/1964-olympic-skating-pair-only-now-discovering-their-place.html |access-date=January 12, 2014}}</ref>

=== Speed skating ===
[[File:Lidiya Skoblikova 1967.jpg|thumb|right|[[Lidia Skoblikova]] in 1967.]]

{{Main|Speed skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}

The [[speed skating]] events took place on an outdoor track set up around the [[Olympiahalle (Innsbruck)|Olympiaeisstadion]]. While the Soviets dominated the women's events, the men's podiums are more international.<ref name="Speed Skating at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games">{{cite web |title=Speed Skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/SSK |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

The American [[Terry McDermott (speed skater)|Terry McDermott]], who was not one of the favorites, won the men's 500 meters setting a new Olympic record. Taking part in his first international competition, he borrowed skates from his trainer [[Leo Freisinger]]. Three athletes, including the favorite of the event [[Yevgeny Grishin (speed skater)|Yevgeny Grishin]], shared second place.<ref>{{cite web |title=500 metres, Men – Speed Skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1013 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> The Soviet [[Ants Antson]] won the gold medal in the 1,500 meters, ahead of the Dutch [[Kees Verkerk]] and the Norwegian [[Villy Haugen]], after a very close race.<ref>{{cite web |title=1,500 metres, Men – Speed Skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1014 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> The Norwegians score a hat-trick in the 5,000 meters. [[Knut Johannesen]] is a gold medalist beating the Olympic record just two-tenths ahead of [[Per Ivar Moe]].<ref>{{harvsp | Wallechinsky | 2001 | p = 114}}</ref> Finally, the Swede [[Jonny Nilsson]] won the 10,000 meters ahead of the Norwegians [[Fred Anton Maier]] and Knut Johannesen. This race was controversial because Nilsson was one of the few to skate before the wind picked up, and enjoyed better ice than most of the other competitors.<ref name="Valle p.100" /><ref>{{harvsp | Wallechinsky | 2001 | p = 121}}</ref>

[[File:Irina Yegorova, Lidiya Skoblikova, Kaija Mustonen 1964.jpg|thumb|left|[[Irina Yegorova]], [[Lidiya Skoblikova]], and [[Kaija Mustonen]] on the podium during the 1964 Winter Olympics, ]]

The Soviet [[Lidia Skoblikova]] won all four races at the 1963 world championships. A big favorite, she reproduced the same performance at the 1964 Olympic Games, breaking the Olympic record each time. She thus becomes the first athlete to win four gold medals in one edition of the Winter Games and the first, after her two titles in 1960, to accumulate six gold medals in several editions. Skoblikova first won the 500 meters ahead of her compatriots [[Irina Yegorova]] and [[Tatyana Sidorova]]. On 1,000 meters, she was ahead of Irina Iegorova and the Finn [[Kaija Mustonen]]. She dominated the 1,500 meters, with a time almost three seconds ahead of Mustonen.<ref>{{harvsp | Monnin | 2010 | p = 73}}</ref><ref>{{harvsp | Wallechinsky | 2001 | pp = 125–138}}</ref> Finally, Skoblikova took the 5,000 meters with almost four seconds. The North Korean [[Han Pil-hwa]], unknown before the Games, created a surprise: tied with Skoblikova halfway through the course, she was ended up tied for second with the Soviet [[Valentina Stenina]]. North Korea participated in the Games for the first time; that was the country's first Olympic medal.<ref>{{cite web |title=3,000 metres, Women – Speed Skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1020 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> Upon her return home, Skoblikova was made a member of the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union|Communist Party]] and became the first woman to win the title of Soviet Sportsman of the Year.<ref name="Adams p.348 ">{{harvsp | Adams | 2004 | p = 348}}</ref>

=== Ski jumping ===
{{Main|Ski jumping at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}

[[File:Veikko Kankkonen, Toralf Engan and Torgeir Brandtzaeg 1964.jpg|thumb|left|[[Toralf Engan]], [[Veikko Kankkonen]] and [[Torgeir Brandtzaeg]], medalists for Large hill individual at 1964 Olympics]]
[[File:A view of the Bergisel ski jump from the 1964 Winter Olympics, Innsbruck, Austria.jpg|thumb|'''A view of the Bergisel ski jump from the 1964 Winter Olympics, Innsbruck, Austria. Image taken in June 1966''']]
For the first time in 1964, two [[ski jumping]] events were contested at the Olympic Games: small hill, contested at [[Toni-Seelos-Olympiaschanze]] and big hill, which takes place at [[Bergisel Ski Jump]]. They have a [[construction point]] of 70 and 90 meters respectively. Athletes jump three times and their two best results count in each event.<ref name="Adams p.347" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Ski Jumping at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/SKJ |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021 |archive-date=8 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210608170851/https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/SKJ |url-status=dead}}</ref>

The Czechoslovak [[Josef Matouš]] surprised many by winning the first round of the normal hill while the Finn [[Veikko Kankkonen]], who was among the favorites, was only twenty-ninth. Kankkonen had the best jump of the competition in the second set, at 80 meters, and the Norwegian [[Toralf Engan]] took the lead. After the third round, Kankkonen who again produced a good jump, became Olympic champion. Toralf Engan was second while young Norwegian [[Torgeir Brandtzæg]] took third place.<ref>{{cite web |title=Normal Hill, Individual, Men – Ski Jumping at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/2374 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> In the first round of the big hill, Veikko Kankkonen took the lead in front of Toralf Engan with a jump of 95.5 meters. Engan took the first place after the second jump, while Kankkonen and Brandtzæg followed closely behind. Brandtzæg finished with a good jump unlike his two rivals. The medalists are the same as for the normal hill, but this time Engan is Olympic champion ahead of Kankkonen.<ref>{{cite web |title=Large Hill, Individual, Men – Ski Jumping at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/2378 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

=== Alpine skiing ===
[[File:Marielle Goitschel.JPG|thumb|right|[[Marielle Goitschel]] in 2008.]]

{{Main|Alpine skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}

Most [[alpine skiing]] events were held at [[Axamer Lizum]], with the men's downhill being held at the [[Patscherkofel]] (above [[Igls]]). Three events were on the program for men and women: [[Downhill (ski competition)|downhill]], [[giant slalom]] and [[Slalom skiing|slalom]]. For the first time at the Olympics, athletes were timed to the hundredth of a second. The competition was held in mourning for the death of Australian Ross Milne, who crashed into a tree during downhill training.<ref name="Adams p.347" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Alpine Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/ASK |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021 |archive-date=8 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210608170850/https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/ASK |url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[Egon Zimmermann]] of Austria won the men's downhill, 74 hundredths of a second ahead of France's [[Léo Lacroix]] and 1.32 seconds over [[Wolfgang Bartels]] of Germany.<ref>{{cite web |title=Downhill, Men – Alpine Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1224 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> For the last time at the Olympics, the men's giant slalom was held in a single round. The French [[François Bonlieu]] won the race ahead of the Austrian favorites: [[Karl Schranz]] was second, and [[Josef Stiegler]] was third.<ref>{{harvsp | Wallechinsky | 2001 | pp = 201–202}}</ref> For the first time, the Olympic slalom had a two-round qualifying phase. The 25 best take part in the two final rounds which determine the ranking of the event. Austrian officials tried to replace Josef Stiegler with Egon Zimmermann, but Stiegler competed in the slalom under public pressure. He finally won the event. The Americans [[Billy Kidd]] and [[Jimmy Heuga]], second and third respectively, won their country's first Olympic medals in alpine skiing.<ref>{{cite web |title=Slalom, Men – Alpine Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1226 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref><ref>{{harvsp | Wallechinsky | 2001 | p = 208}}</ref>

In the women's downhill, the Austrians achieved the second treble in the history of the Winter Games in alpine skiing. The favorite [[Christl Haas]] was Olympic champion, more than a second ahead of [[Edith Zimmermann]] and [[Traudl Hecher]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Downhill, Women – Alpine Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1233 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> The technical events were dominated by two French women, the Goitschel sisters. [[Marielle Goitschel]], aged 18, won the first round of the slalom ahead of her sister [[Christine Goitschel|Christine]], one year her senior. Christine was the fastest, however, in the second run. She won gold, ahead of Marielle, while the bronze medal was awarded to the American [[Jean Saubert]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Slalom, Women – Alpine Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1235 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> Two days later, Christine Goitschel took the lead in the giant slalom. His time was then equaled by Jean Saubert. Marielle Goitschel, the fourteenth skier to set off, was almost a second ahead of them however. The eldest Goitschel finished first this time, while her sister shared second place with Saubert.<ref>{{cite web |title=Giant Slalom, Women – Alpine Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1234 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

=== Cross-country skiing ===
[[File:Sixten Jernberg, Innsbruck 1964.jpg|thumb|right|[[Sixten Jernberg]] during the 1964 Olympics.]]

{{Main|Cross-country skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics}}

The [[cross-country skiing (sport)|cross-country skiing]] events took place near the village of [[Seefeld in Tirol]]. The men competed as usual in individual over 15, 30 and 50 kilometer as well as in the 4 × 10 kilometer relay. On the other hand, women competed for the first time at the Olympic Games the 5 kilometer, introduced at the world championships in 1962, in addition to the 10 kilometer and the relay 3 × 5 kilometer.<ref name="Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games">{{cite web |title=Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/editions/37/sports/CCS |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

Men's events started with the 30 kilometers. The Finn [[Eero Mäntyranta]] won the race ahead of the Norwegian [[Harald Grønningen]] and the Soviet [[Igor Voronchikhin]]. The Swede [[Sixten Jernberg]], the favorite after his six Olympic medals obtained in [[Cross-country skiing at the 1956 Winter Olympics|1956]] and [[Cross-country skiing at the 1960 Winter Olympics|1960]], finished fifth. Eight of the top nine athletes were Scandinavian.<ref>{{harvsp | Monnin | 2010 | pp = 73–74}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=30 kilometres, Men – Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1937 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> In the 15 kilometer skied three days later, Eero Mäntyranta was once again crowned Olympic champion ahead of Harald Grønningen. Sixten Jernberg wins bronze, his seventh Olympic medal.<ref>{{cite web |title=15 kilometres, Men – Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1936 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> Racing the day before his 35th birthday, Jernberg took the lead at the end of the 50 kilometer. He won gold, his eighth Olympic medal, finishing more than a minute ahead of his compatriot [[Assar Rönnlund]].<ref>{{cite web |title=50 kilometres, Men – Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1938 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> The end of the relay 4 × 10 kilometer was a duel between the Finnish Eero Mäntyranta and the Swede Assar Rönnlund, who overtook the Soviet [[Pavel Kolchin]] one kilometer from the finish. Sweden eventually won the event, eight seconds ahead of Finland and twelve over the Soviet Union. Jernberg ended his Olympic career with nine medals including four gold, which was a new record.<ref>{{cite web |title=4 × 10 kilometres Relay, Men – Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1939 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.olympedia.org/athletes/87535 |title=Sixten Jernberg |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

Soviet skiers dominated the women's events as they won six of the seven possible medals.<ref name="Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games" /> In the 10 kilometer they achieved the treble as in 1960: [[Klavdiya Boyarskikh]] ahead [[Yevdokiya Mekshilo]] and [[Maria Gusakova]]. For the first time among women, non-European cross-country skiers took part in the Olympic Games. The two North Koreans and the two Mongols, however, finished in the last four places.<ref name="Monnin p.75">{{harvsp | Monnin | 2010 | p = 75}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=10 kilometres, Women – Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1944 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> Boyarskikh also won the very close Olympic 5&nbsp;km, while Finland's [[Mirja Lehtonen]] surprised by taking second place. The Soviet [[Alevtina Kolchina]] was third.<ref>{{cite web |title=5 kilometres, Women – Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1943 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> Finally, the Soviets won the relay 3 × 5 kilometer for the first time. They were well ahead of the Swedes by two minutes and the Finns by three.<ref>{{cite web |title=3 × 5 kilometres Relay, Women – Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics |url=https://www.olympedia.org/results/1945 |website=Olympedia |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref> Klavdiya Boyarskikh wins his third gold medal at these Games.<ref name="Cross Country Skiing at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games" />

== Closing Ceremony ==
For the first time on games history, the Closing Ceremony was not held at the Olympic Stadium and in an indoor place, took place on February 9 at the [[Olympiahalle (Innsbruck)|Olympiaeisstadion]].<ref name="universalis chronology" /> The flags of Greece, the founding nation of the Olympic Games, Austria, the host country, and France, the host country of the next Games, were raised to the sound of the national anthems. The President of the {{abbreviation | IOC | International Olympic Committee}} [[Avery Brundage]] officially declared the Games closed before the extinction of the [[Olympic flame]].<ref>{{harvsp | Wolfgang | Neumann | 1967 | pp = 335–336}}</ref>

== Games highlights ==
* The games were opened by a concert performed by [[Vienna Philharmonic]], under the baton of [[Karl Böhm]]. [[Beethoven]]'s [[Symphony No. 7 (Beethoven)|7th Symphony]] and [[Mozart]]'s [[Symphony No. 40 (Mozart)|40th Symphony]] were performed in the opening concert.
* Normally snowy, Innsbruck was threatened by a lack of snow. The Austrian army carved out 20,000 ice bricks from a mountain top and transported them to the bobsled and luge runs. They also carried 40,000 cubic meters of snow to the Alpine skiing courses. The army packed down the slopes by hand and foot.<ref name=Olympics>[http://www.olympic.org/uk/games/past/index_uk.asp?OLGT=2&OLGY=1964 www.Olympic.org]</ref><!-- Most of the highlights are from this source. --> (A heavy snowfall occurred immediately after {{nowrap|the Games.)<ref name=ahsfc>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=TFpYAAAAIBAJ&sjid=bPcDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6141%2C2295861 |work=Spokane Daily Chronicle |location= Washington |agency=Associated Press |title=Athletes quit Olympics site |date=February 11, 1964 |page=15}}</ref>}}
* [[Lidia Skoblikova]] won all of the women's speed skating events.
* Italian bobsleigh pilot [[Eugenio Monti]] distinguished himself by helping Britain's [[Tony Nash (bobsleigh)|Tony Nash]] and [[Robin Dixon]] to win the gold medals when he loaned them an axle bolt to replace one that was broken. The Italians took bronze, but Monti was honored as the first recipient of the [[International Fair Play Committee]]'s Pierre de Coubertin World Trophy for sportsmanship.
* [[Egon Zimmermann]] of [[Austria]] took the gold medal in the men's downhill alpine skiing event.
* In the 4-man bobsled, the Canadian team won the gold medal with a total winning time of 4:14.46.
* Norway's [[Knut Johannesen]] won the men's 5,000&nbsp;m speed skating event in an Olympic record time of 7:38.40.
* [[Klavdiya Boyarskikh]] of the USSR earned three gold medals in cross-country skiing and, on the men's side, Finnish [[Eero Mäntyranta]] won two and earned the nickname "Mr. Seefeld" after the venue because of his domination.
* In alpine skiing, French sisters [[Christine Goitschel|Christine]] and [[Marielle Goitschel]] finished first and second in both the slalom and the giant slalom.
* Ski jumping gained a second event, and the sport of [[luge]] made its Olympic debut.
* Politically, the Games were notable because East and West Germany entered a combined team for the last time.
* For the first time the Closing Ceremonies were held at a different place than the Opening Ceremonies.This also the first time that an Olympic Ceremonies are held in an indoor venue.

== Medals ==
[[File:1964 Winter Olympics medals.JPG|thumb|right|The medals of the Innsbruck Games.]]
Fourteen of the thirty-six nations which participated in these Games won at least one medal, as detailed in the table below. Already first in [[1956 Winter Olympic Games|1956]] and [[1960 Winter Olympic Games|1960]], the [[Soviet Union at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Soviet Union]] came far ahead of this table with twenty-five medals: eleven gold, eight silver and six bronze, a new record for both gold and total medals won at a single Winter Olympics. The host country, ninth four years earlier, was second with twelve medals, including seven in [[# Alpine skiing|alpine skiing]]. Norway, fourth in 1964, came third with fifteen medals.<ref name=universalis /><ref name="1964 Innsbruck Winter Games" /><ref>{{harvsp | Mogore | 1989 | p = 102}}</ref>

=== Most decorated athletes ===
{{Main|List of 1964 Winter Olympics medal winners}}

The Soviets also dominated the ranking of the most medal-winning athletes as the speed skater [[Lidia Skoblikova]] and cross-country skier [[Klavdiya Boyarskikh]] came first and second.<ref name="1964 Innsbruck Winter Games" />

== Venues ==
{{Main|Venues of the 1964 Winter Olympics}}

[[File:12-06-05-innsbruck-by-ralfr-171.jpg|thumb|left|The men's descent takes place on the slopes of the [[Patscherkofel]].]]

Several sports venues were built especially for the Games. New slopes for [[Alpine skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics|alpine skiing]] were developed near the village of [[Axamer Lizum]], about twenty kilometers from Innsbruck. There is a [[Olympic Sliding Centre Innsbruck|bobsleigh and luge track]] in [[Igls]], seven kilometers south of Innsbruck. The runway, 1506 meters long, had 14 curves and a drop of 138 meters.<ref name="Adams p.346">{{harvsp | Adams | 2004 | p = 346}}</ref><ref name="Bobsleigh at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games" /> For the first time at the Games, the bobsleigh track used artificial ice.<ref name=cio /> The [[Olympiahalle (Innsbruck)|Olympiaeisstadion]], an eleven thousand-seat ice rink completed in 1963 and located in the center of Innsbruck, hosted the competitions of [[Figure skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics|figure skating]] and most games of [[Ice hockey at the 1964 Winter Olympics|ice hockey]]. The other hockey matches were played at the [[Messehalle (Innsbruck)|Messehalle]]. The [[Speed skating at the 1964 Winter Olympics|speed skating]] ring, made of artificial ice, was installed outside the Olympiaeisstadion.<ref name=universalis /><ref name="Ice Hockey at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games" /><ref name="Speed Skating at the 1964 Innsbruck Winter Games" />

[[File:OL Innsbruck 1964 500m skøyter Gull - L0029 453bFo30141606080117.jpg|thumb|[[Eisschnellaufbahn]]]]

The [[Ski jumping at the 1964 Winter Olympics|ski jumping]] events were held on the [[Toni-Seelos-Olympiaschanze]] (normal hill) at [[Seefeld in Tirol]] and the [[Bergisel Ski Jump]] (big jump) in Innsbruck. The Bergisel ski jump, built in wood in 1920, was replaced by a concrete ski jump. The [[Cross-country skiing at the 1964 Winter Olympics|cross-country skiing]] and [[Biathlon at the 1964 Winter Olympics|biathlon]] tracks were located in Seefeld, like the small hill.<ref>{{harvsp | Wolfgang | Neumann | 1967 | pp = 22–23}}</ref><ref name=universalis /> The opening ceremony was celebrated at the foot of the Bergisel ski jump while the closing ceremony took place at the Olympiaeisstadion.<ref name="universalis chronology" /> An Olympic Village consisting of eight eleven-storey buildings was built outside the city.<ref name="Adams p.346" />

* [[Axamer Lizum]] – Alpine skiing (except the men's downhill)
* [[Bergiselschanze]] – opening ceremonies and ski jumping (large hill)
* [[Olympic Sliding Centre Innsbruck|Bob und Rodelbahn Igls]] – bobsleigh, luge
* [[Eisschnellaufbahn]] – speed skating
* [[Messehalle (Innsbruck)|Messehalle]] – ice hockey
* [[Olympiahalle (Innsbruck)|Olympiahalle]] – closing ceremonies, figure skating, ice hockey
* [[Patscherkofel]] – Alpine skiing (men's downhill)
* [[Seefeld, Tirol|Seefeld]] – biathlon, cross-county skiing, Nordic combined, ski jumping (normal hill)

== Participating nations ==
A total of 36 nations sent athletes to Innsbruck, six more than in [[Squaw Valley Ski Resort|Squaw Valley]] in [[1960 Winter Olympic Games|1960]]. The total number of athletes was 1,091, up from 665 four years earlier.<ref name=universalis /> [[Mongolia at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Mongolia]], [[India at the 1964 Winter Olympics|India]] and [[North Korea at the 1964 Winter Olympics|North Korea]] participated in the Winter Games for the first time. [[Belgium at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Belgium]], [[Greece at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Greece]], [[Iran at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Iran]], [[Romania at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Romania]] and [[Yugoslavia at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Yugoslavia]] returned to this competition after missing it in 1960. On the other hand, South Africa and New Zealand, which took part in Squaw Valley, did not compete in Innsbruck. Athletes from [[West Germany]] (FRG) and [[German Democratic Republic|East Germany]] (GDR) competed together as [[United Team of Germany at the Olympics|Unified Team Germany]] from 1956 to 1964.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.olympedia.org/countries |title=Olympic Countries |work=Olympedia.org |access-date=June 8, 2021}}</ref>

The number indicated in brackets is the number of athletes entered in the official events for each country.<ref name="1964 Innsbruck Winter Games">{{cite web |url=http://www.olympedia.org/editions/37 |title=1964 Innsbruck Winter Games |work=Olympedia.org |access-date=June 8, 2021}}</ref>

== Prior fatalities ==
Two fatal events before the 1964 Winter Olympics affected the outcome and mood of the Games:

* [[Australia at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Australian]] alpine skier [[Ross Milne (alpine skier)|Ross Milne]] and [[Great Britain at the 1964 Winter Olympics|British]] luge slider [[Kazimierz Kay-Skrzypeski|Kazimierz "Kay" Skrzypecki]] died during training shortly before the Games.<ref name="NYT19640126">{{cite news |title=Milne, 19, Loses Control at 60 M.P.H. and Runs into Tree in Drill |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/01/26/archives/milne-19-loses-control-at-60-mph-and-runs-into-tree-in-driii.html |access-date=8 June 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=January 26, 1964 |location=Innsbruck}}</ref><ref name="Haid1965">{{cite journal |last1=Haid |first1=Bruno C. |title=Medical Service During the Winter Olympic Games...1964...Innsbruck, Austria |journal=Anesthesia & Analgesia |date=March 1965 |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=240–244 |pmid=14284268 |issn=0003-2999}}</ref> The organizing committee said that Ross crashed into a tree during a training run. The [[International Olympic Committee|IOC]] suggested that inexperience might have played a role in Ross's death. Manager John Wagner suggested that overcrowding played a role, saying that Milne had tried to slow down "on a spot which was not prepared for stopping or swinging" to avoid a crowd of contestants. His brother [[Malcolm Milne]] competed at the [[1968 Winter Olympics|1968]] and [[1972 Winter Olympics]].
* On February 15, 1961, the entire [[U.S. Figure Skating|United States figure skating team]] and several family members, coaches, and officials were killed when [[Sabena Flight 548]] crashed in [[Brussels]], Belgium, en route to the World Championships in [[Prague]]. The accident caused the cancellation of the 1961 World Championships and necessitated the building of a new American skating program. Although American figure skaters were still too young in 1964 (most were aged 15 or lower), they still managed to win two medals.<ref name=acftst>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Y6BWAAAAIBAJ&pg=6629%2C4868375 |title=Air Crash Fatal to 73 Is Probed – Jet's Plunge Kills Skaters |date=February 16, 1961 |page=1 |newspaper=[[The Spokesman-Review]] |access-date=February 19, 2014}}</ref><ref name="StillCrystalClear">{{Cite news |url=https://www.espn.com/espn/eticket/story?page=110215/skatingcrash&redirected=true |title=Still Crystal Clear |quote=The plane crash that killed the 1961 U.S. world championship figure skating team decimated families and the sport, but alongside grief came renewal. |last=Ford |first=Bonnie D. |year=2011 |publisher=[[ESPN]] |access-date=February 19, 2014}}</ref>

There were also several injuries which occurred prior to the event.
* [[Liechtenstein at the 1964 Winter Olympics|Liechtenstein]] Alpine skiers [[Wolfgang Ender]] broke his leg and [[Edmund Schaedler]] fractured his arm in a crash close to the same location as Australian Milne, only a few minutes after the fatality occurred.<ref name="NYT19640126" /><ref name="Haid1965" />
* [[United Team of Germany at the 1964 Winter Olympics|German]] tobogganer [[Josef Fleischmann]] crashed during practices.<ref name="NYT19640126" /><ref name="Haid1965" />

== After the Games ==

=== After the Games ===
In the 1970s, the American city of [[Denver]], chosen to host the [[1976 Winter Olympics]], rejected the bid after a statewide referendum. About ten cities applied to take over the Games and Innsbruck was selected. The main reasons for this choice were the venues built for the 1964 Games, which kept costs down, and their good organization during the 1964 Olympics.<ref>{{harvsp | Adams | 2004 | p = 368}}</ref> The Olympic venues subsequently hosted various sports competitions such as the [[Four Hills Tournament]], Bobsleigh and Luge World Cup events, the [[2005 Winter Universiade|Winter Universiade]] and the [[2005 Men's Ice Hockey World Championships|Ice Hockey World Championship]] in 2005 and the [[2012 Winter Youth Olympic Games|first Winter Youth Olympic Games in 2012]].<ref>{{cite web |language=de |url=http://diepresse.com/home/panorama/oesterreich/539500/Zweimal-Olympia-und-was-jetztInnsbruck_Zweimal-Olympia-und-was-jetzt |title=Innsbruck: Zweimal Olympia, und was jetzt? |trans-title=Innsbruck: Two Olympics, and now what? |author=Manuel Fasser |work=[[Die Presse]] |date=February 13, 2010 |access-date=August 3, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.olympic.org/fr/news/innsbruck-beneficie-d-une-nouvelle-generation-de-legs-olympiques/218375 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202161119/http://www.olympic.org/fr/news/innsbruck-beneficie-d-une-nouvelle-generation-de-legs-olympiques/218375 |trans-title=Innsbruck benefits from a new generation of Olympic legacies |title=Innsbruck bénéficie d'une nouvelle génération de legs olympiques |language=French |publisher=International Olympic Committee |date=12 December 2013 |archive-date=2014-02-02 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
